question: Build a counter component with increment, decrement, and reset buttons.
thoughtProcess: This is the classic warm-up. The interviewer wants to see that I understand useState and event handlers. I'll keep a single number in state. For the updates I'll use the functional updater form, setCount(c => c + 1), because it's the correct pattern when the new value depends on the previous value and avoids stale-state bugs if multiple updates batch. Reset just sets it back to the initial value. I'll keep the markup minimal and accessible with clear button labels.
lineByLine: useState(0) creates the count state initialized to zero and gives us the setter. increment and decrement use the functional updater form (c) => c +/- 1, which reads the latest value from React rather than the possibly stale count variable captured in the closure. reset sets the value directly to 0. In the JSX we display the count and wire each button's onClick to the matching handler.
timeComplexity: O(1) per update; each click triggers one state update and a single re-render.
spaceComplexity: O(1); a single number is stored in state.

alternativeApproaches.title: useReducer for grouped logic
alternativeApproaches.explanation: If the counter grew more actions or rules, like min/max bounds, a reducer centralizes the transitions and is easier to test.

followUps.question: Why use the functional updater form instead of setCount(count + 1)?
followUps.answer: Because React batches state updates and the count variable in the closure reflects the value at render time, not after pending updates. If you call setCount(count + 1) twice in one handler, both read the same stale count and you only increment once. setCount(c => c + 1) reads the latest queued value each time, so consecutive updates compose correctly.

followUps.question: How would you prevent the count from going below zero?
followUps.answer: Clamp in the updater: setCount(c => Math.max(0, c - 1)) for decrement. With a reducer you'd add the bound in the 'dec' case. You could also disable the decrement button when count is 0 by setting its disabled prop, giving the user clear feedback that the action is unavailable.

question: Build a controlled form with validation for name and email, showing errors on submit.
thoughtProcess: I'll make this a controlled form so React state is the single source of truth for each field. I'll store values in one state object and errors in another. Validation runs on submit: name is required, email must match a basic pattern. If there are errors I prevent submission and display them; otherwise I call onSubmit with the values. I'll also validate on change after the first submit attempt so the user gets live feedback while fixing mistakes, which is a nice UX touch. I must remember to call e.preventDefault to stop the native form submission and page reload.
lineByLine: values holds both field values keyed by input name, errors holds validation messages, and submitted tracks whether the user has tried to submit so we only show live errors afterward. validate is a pure function returning an errors object. handleChange updates the matching field using the input's name attribute as the key, then re-validates if the form was already submitted. handleSubmit calls e.preventDefault to stop the page reload, marks submitted, validates, and only proceeds if the errors object is empty. The JSX wires each input as controlled via value and onChange, and conditionally renders error messages with role alert for accessibility.
timeComplexity: O(n) per validation where n is the number of fields; here constant.
spaceComplexity: O(n) for storing field values and errors.

alternativeApproaches.title: Validate on blur instead of on submit
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Validating each field when it loses focus gives earlier feedback per field without waiting for submit, often a better UX for longer forms. You track touched fields and only show a field's error once it has been blurred.

alternativeApproaches.title: Use a form library
alternativeApproaches.explanation: In production, libraries like React Hook Form or Formik handle controlled state, validation schemas, and performance optimizations like uncontrolled inputs, reducing boilerplate for complex forms.

followUps.question: What is the difference between a controlled and uncontrolled input?
followUps.answer: A controlled input's value is driven by React state via the value prop, so React is the single source of truth and you read the value from state. An uncontrolled input keeps its value in the DOM and you read it via a ref when needed, using defaultValue for the initial value. Controlled inputs make validation and conditional logic easy; uncontrolled ones reduce re-renders and boilerplate for simple cases.

followUps.question: Why do you call e.preventDefault in handleSubmit?
followUps.answer: By default, submitting a form triggers a full page navigation or reload, which would discard the React app's state. Calling e.preventDefault stops that native behavior so you can handle the submission in JavaScript, validate, and send data via fetch without reloading the page.

question: Build a todo list with add, toggle complete, and delete.
thoughtProcess: I need an array of todo objects in state, each with a stable id, text, and done flag. The id is important because I'll use it as the React key and to target toggles and deletes, never the array index, since the list mutates. Adding pushes a new object with a generated id and clears the input. Toggling maps over the array and flips done for the matching id. Deleting filters out the matching id. I'll keep the new-todo input controlled. I'll generate ids with a counter or crypto.randomUUID so they're unique and stable.
lineByLine: todos is the array of items and text is the controlled input value. addTodo prevents the form reload, ignores empty input, appends a new immutable todo with a unique id, and clears the input. toggle maps the array and returns a new object with done flipped for the matching id, leaving others unchanged. remove filters out the target id. In the JSX each li uses the stable t.id as its key, a checkbox bound to t.done toggles via onChange, and a Delete button removes the item. All updates create new arrays and objects rather than mutating, which is required for React to detect changes.
timeComplexity: O(n) for toggle and delete since they map or filter the list; O(1) amortized for add.
spaceComplexity: O(n) for the list of todos.

alternativeApproaches.title: useReducer for the todo actions
alternativeApproaches.explanation: As features grow, like editing, filtering, and clearing completed, a reducer with action types centralizes the state transitions and is easier to test than scattered setTodos calls.

alternativeApproaches.title: Persist to localStorage
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Wrap the state in a useLocalStorage hook or sync with an effect so todos survive a page refresh, a common follow-up requirement.

followUps.question: Why use a stable id as the key instead of the array index?
followUps.answer: Because the list changes order and items are deleted from the middle, index keys would cause React to associate the wrong DOM node and component state with each row, leading to bugs like a checkbox state appearing on the wrong todo after a delete, plus unnecessary re-renders. A stable id keyed on the item itself lets React correctly track each row across changes.

followUps.question: Why do you create new arrays and objects instead of mutating the existing state?
followUps.answer: React detects changes by comparing references. If you mutate the existing array or object in place, the reference stays the same and React may not re-render, or memoized children won't update. Returning new arrays with map, filter, and spread, and new objects with spread, gives React new references to detect, which is the immutable update pattern React relies on.

question: Build a search filter that filters a list of items as the user types.
thoughtProcess: I have a list of items and a search query in state. The filtered list is derived data, so I compute it during render rather than storing it in separate state, which avoids a sync bug where the filtered list and query drift apart. I'll do a case-insensitive substring match. The input is controlled. If the list were large, I'd memoize the filter with useMemo, but for a small list deriving on each render is fine and simplest. I'll handle the empty-results case with a message.
lineByLine: query holds the controlled search text. filtered is derived on each render by filtering items with a case-insensitive includes check, trimming the query first. We deliberately do not store filtered in state, because it is fully determined by items and query; deriving it avoids state that can fall out of sync. The input is controlled via value and onChange. The JSX shows a No matches message when the filtered list is empty, otherwise renders the list with each item as the key, which is fine here assuming items are unique strings.
timeComplexity: O(n * m) where n is the number of items and m is the average string length, recomputed each render.

alternativeApproaches.title: Memoize the filter for large lists
alternativeApproaches.explanation: If items is large or the filter is expensive, wrap it in useMemo keyed on items and query so it only recomputes when those change.

alternativeApproaches.title: Debounce for server-side search
alternativeApproaches.explanation: If matching requires a network call rather than filtering an in-memory list, debounce the query so you don't fire a request on every keystroke.

followUps.question: Why derive the filtered list during render instead of storing it in state?
followUps.answer: The filtered list is fully determined by the source items and the query, so it is derived data, not independent state. Storing it separately means you must remember to update it whenever items or query change, and any missed update causes the list and the input to drift out of sync. Computing it during render keeps a single source of truth and eliminates that class of bug.

followUps.question: When would you add useMemo here?
followUps.answer: When the items list is large or the filtering logic is expensive, and the component re-renders for reasons unrelated to query or items, so the filter would otherwise rerun needlessly. useMemo keyed on items and query confines the recomputation to when those inputs actually change. For a small list, the memoization overhead isn't worth it and plain derivation is clearer.

question: Build a debounced search input that calls an API only after the user stops typing.
thoughtProcess: The key idea is to separate the immediate input value, which updates on every keystroke for responsiveness, from the debounced value that actually triggers the fetch. I'll keep the raw query in state and derive a debounced version with a useEffect plus setTimeout: on each query change I set a timer, and the cleanup clears the previous timer, so the debounced value only updates after the user pauses. A second effect fetches whenever the debounced value changes. I must handle cleanup to avoid setting state after unmount and to cancel stale requests, and I should ignore out-of-order responses. I'll use an AbortController for cancellation.
lineByLine: query is the immediate controlled value; debounced lags behind it. The first effect runs on every query change: it schedules setDebounced after 300ms and its cleanup clears that timer, so rapid keystrokes keep resetting the timer and debounced only updates once typing pauses. The second effect runs when debounced changes: it short-circuits for an empty query, creates an AbortController, sets loading, fetches with the abort signal, stores results, ignores AbortError, and clears loading in finally. Its cleanup aborts the in-flight request when debounced changes again or on unmount, which both cancels wasted work and prevents out-of-order responses from overwriting fresh ones.
timeComplexity: O(1) per keystroke for scheduling; network cost dominates per actual request.
spaceComplexity: O(n) for storing the results list.

alternativeApproaches.title: Extract a reusable useDebounce hook
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Move the debounce effect into a custom hook so any component can debounce a value, keeping the search component focused on fetching.

alternativeApproaches.title: Use a data-fetching library
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Tools like TanStack Query or SWR handle caching, deduplication, cancellation, and loading and error states, so you debounce the key and let the library manage the request lifecycle.

followUps.question: Why is the cleanup function in the debounce effect essential?
followUps.answer: The cleanup runs before the effect runs again and on unmount. In the debounce effect it clears the previous timer, which is what actually produces the debounce: without it, every keystroke would schedule its own setDebounced and they'd all fire. In the fetch effect, the cleanup aborts the in-flight request, preventing wasted network work and stopping a stale response from a previous query from overwriting the current results.

followUps.question: How does this prevent out-of-order or stale responses?
followUps.answer: Each time the debounced value changes, the fetch effect's cleanup aborts the previous request before starting the new one. So an older request that was still in flight is cancelled and its AbortError is ignored, meaning only the latest request's response can update state. This avoids the race where a slow earlier response arrives after a faster later one and shows wrong results.

question: Build an accordion where each section can expand and collapse independently.
thoughtProcess: An accordion is a list of sections each with a header and collapsible body. I'll take the sections as data and track which ones are open. For independent open sections, a Set of open indices or ids works well. Clicking a header toggles its id in the set. I'll render the body only when open, or use CSS to hide it; rendering conditionally is simpler. I should add accessibility: the header is a button with aria-expanded, and aria-controls pointing at the panel. A common variant is single-open mode, which I'll mention as an alternative.
lineByLine: openIds is a Set of the currently open section ids, lazily initialized so a new empty Set isn't allocated on every render. toggle copies the set immutably, removes the id if present or adds it otherwise, and returns the new set; copying is required so React sees a new reference. In the render we map each section, compute isOpen from the set, and render a header button with aria-expanded and aria-controls for accessibility. The panel is rendered only when isOpen is true, and it gets a matching id and role region so assistive tech can associate it with its header.
timeComplexity: O(1) per toggle using a Set; O(n) to render n sections.
spaceComplexity: O(k) where k is the number of open sections stored in the set.

alternativeApproaches.title: Single-open accordion
alternativeApproaches.explanation: If only one section may be open at a time, store a single openId instead of a set and set it to the clicked id, or to null if it was already open.

alternativeApproaches.title: CSS-based collapse with animation
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Instead of conditional rendering, keep the panel mounted and animate max-height or use a details/summary element, which gives smooth transitions and keeps content in the DOM for in-page search.

followUps.question: Why store open sections in a Set and copy it on each toggle?
followUps.answer: A Set gives O(1) membership checks and toggling, which reads cleanly for many independently open sections. We copy it into a new Set before mutating because React detects state changes by reference; mutating the existing Set in place would keep the same reference and React might not re-render. Creating a new Set gives a fresh reference for React to detect.

followUps.question: How would you make the accordion accessible?
followUps.answer: Use a real button for each header so it is keyboard and screen-reader friendly, set aria-expanded to reflect open state, and link the header to its panel with aria-controls and a matching panel id. Give the panel role region or use the proper heading structure. Optionally, use the native details and summary elements, which provide much of this behavior for free.

question: Build a tabs component that shows one panel at a time.
thoughtProcess: Tabs need a list of tab labels and corresponding panels, plus state for which tab is active. I'll store the active index or id. Clicking a tab sets it active. Only the active panel renders. For accessibility I'll use role tablist, tab, and tabpanel, set aria-selected on the active tab, and ideally support arrow-key navigation, though I'll keep the core simple and mention keyboard handling as an enhancement. I'll take tabs as data so the component is reusable.
lineByLine: activeId is initialized to the first tab's id using optional chaining in case tabs is empty. activeTab is derived by finding the tab matching activeId, so we never store the panel content in separate state. The tablist renders a button per tab with role tab and aria-selected reflecting whether it is active; clicking sets activeId. Below, a single tabpanel renders only the active tab's content. Deriving activeTab rather than storing it keeps a single source of truth in activeId.
timeComplexity: O(n) to render n tabs and to find the active one.
spaceComplexity: O(1) extra state, just the active id.

alternativeApproaches.title: Keep all panels mounted
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Render every panel but hide inactive ones with CSS. This preserves each panel's internal state and scroll position when switching tabs, at the cost of mounting all of them.

alternativeApproaches.title: Add keyboard navigation
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Handle ArrowLeft and ArrowRight on the tablist to move focus and selection between tabs, and use roving tabindex so only the active tab is in the tab order, matching the WAI-ARIA tabs pattern.

followUps.question: Should inactive tab panels stay mounted or unmount?
followUps.answer: It depends on the requirement. Unmounting inactive panels, as in the solution, saves memory and resets their state, which is fine for simple content. Keeping them mounted but hidden with CSS preserves internal state, form input, and scroll position across tab switches, which matters for things like a half-filled form, but uses more memory and renders everything upfront.

followUps.question: Why derive activeTab instead of storing the active content in state?
followUps.answer: The active content is fully determined by which tab id is active and the tabs data, so it is derived. Storing it separately would create a second source of truth that could drift from activeId. Finding it during render from activeId keeps one source of truth and avoids sync bugs when tabs change.

question: Build a modal dialog that closes on overlay click, close button, and the Escape key.
thoughtProcess: A modal needs an open state controlled by the parent, an overlay, and a content box. I'll close on three triggers: clicking the overlay but not the content, clicking a close button, and pressing Escape. For Escape I add a keydown listener via useEffect that's only active while open, with cleanup to remove it. For the overlay click I check that the event target is the overlay itself, not bubbled from the content, by comparing target to currentTarget. I should also mention focus management and a portal for production, but I'll keep the core focused. I'll guard against rendering when closed.
lineByLine: The effect runs only when isOpen, attaching a keydown listener that calls onClose on Escape and removing it in cleanup, so the listener exists only while the modal is open and is torn down on close or unmount. If isOpen is false we return null and render nothing. The overlay div's onClick checks e.target === e.currentTarget, which is true only when the click landed directly on the overlay and not bubbled up from the content, so clicking inside the dialog does not close it. The close button calls onClose. role dialog and aria-modal mark the content for assistive tech.
timeComplexity: O(1) for open, close, and event handling.

alternativeApproaches.title: Render into a portal
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Use ReactDOM.createPortal to render the modal at the document body so it escapes parent overflow and z-index stacking contexts, which is the standard production approach.

alternativeApproaches.title: Use the native dialog element
alternativeApproaches.explanation: The HTML dialog element with showModal provides backdrop, Escape handling, and focus trapping natively, reducing custom code, though styling and browser support need consideration.

followUps.question: How do you ensure clicking inside the modal content doesn't close it?
followUps.answer: Attach the close handler to the overlay and inside it compare e.target to e.currentTarget. e.currentTarget is the element the handler is attached to, the overlay, while e.target is what was actually clicked. They are equal only when the overlay itself was clicked; clicks inside the dialog have a different target due to event bubbling, so the guard prevents closing.

followUps.question: What accessibility concerns matter for a modal?
followUps.answer: Move focus into the dialog when it opens and return it to the trigger when it closes, trap focus inside while open so Tab doesn't escape to the background, mark the dialog with role dialog and aria-modal true, label it with aria-labelledby or aria-label, and support closing with Escape. Rendering in a portal and making background content inert also helps screen readers ignore the obscured page.

question: Build a star rating component where clicking a star sets the rating.
thoughtProcess: I need state for the selected rating and, for good UX, a separate hover state so the stars fill on hover before clicking. I'll render a fixed number of stars, say five, filling each one if its index is at or below the hover value when hovering, otherwise the selected rating. Clicking a star sets the rating. Mouse enter on a star sets hover, mouse leave on the container clears hover. For accessibility, I'll make the stars buttons with aria-labels, and I could use a radiogroup pattern, but I'll keep it approachable.
lineByLine: The component is controlled: value and onChange come from the parent, and hover is local UI state for the hover preview. stars is an array 1..max built with Array.from. active is hover if hovering, otherwise the committed value, so the display reflects the hover preview when present. Each star is a button: clicking calls onChange with its number, mouse enter sets hover to that number, and the container's mouse leave resets hover to 0. The fill color is gold when the star number is at or below active. aria-label gives each star a meaningful name.
spaceComplexity: O(n) for the star array; O(1) state.

alternativeApproaches.title: Uncontrolled with internal state
alternativeApproaches.explanation: If the parent doesn't need the value live, store the rating internally with useState and expose it via onChange only on commit, simplifying the parent.

alternativeApproaches.title: Support half stars
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Track the cursor position within a star to allow half-star ratings, using a fractional active value and clip-path or two overlaid half icons to render partial fills.

followUps.question: Why keep hover state separate from the rating value?
followUps.answer: The hover state is a transient preview that should show what would be selected if the user clicks, without committing it. Keeping it separate means moving the mouse away restores the actual committed rating, and the parent's value isn't changed until a real click. Merging them would make hovering accidentally change the saved rating.

followUps.question: How would you make this keyboard accessible?
followUps.answer: Use a radiogroup pattern: render the stars as radio inputs or buttons within role radiogroup, let arrow keys move the selection and Space or Enter commit it, and ensure each option has an accessible label like '3 stars'. This lets keyboard and screen-reader users set a rating without a mouse, which the hover-only approach doesn't support.

question: Build pagination for a list, with page numbers and previous/next controls.
thoughtProcess: I'll take the full list and a page size, track the current page in state, and slice the list for the visible page. Total pages is the ceiling of length over page size. The previous and next buttons change the page, clamped to valid bounds and disabled at the ends. I'll render page-number buttons too, highlighting the current one. Slicing the data is derived, so I compute it during render. I'll guard against the page going out of range, for example if the list shrinks, by clamping.
lineByLine: page holds the requested page. totalPages is the ceiling of items over pageSize, at least 1. current clamps page to totalPages so a stale page beyond the range is corrected during render. start computes the slice offset, and pageItems is the derived visible slice. The list renders the current slice keyed by id. Prev and Next are disabled at the boundaries and step the page. The page-number buttons are generated from a 1..totalPages array, with aria-current marking the active page for accessibility.
timeComplexity: O(pageSize) to render a page; slice is O(pageSize). O(totalPages) for the number buttons.

alternativeApproaches.title: Server-side pagination
alternativeApproaches.explanation: For large datasets, fetch one page at a time from the server using page and pageSize query params, so you never load the whole list into memory; the component then drives requests instead of slicing local data.

alternativeApproaches.title: Windowed page numbers
alternativeApproaches.explanation: When there are many pages, show a windowed set like 1 ... 4 5 6 ... 20 with ellipses around the current page rather than rendering every page number, which keeps the control compact.

followUps.question: Why clamp the page during render instead of only in the click handlers?
followUps.answer: Clamping in render guards against the page becoming invalid for reasons outside the buttons, for example if the items list shrinks so totalPages drops below the current page. Computing current as min(page, totalPages) ensures the displayed slice is always valid even if state hasn't been corrected yet, avoiding an empty or out-of-range view. You can also reset page in an effect when items change, but render-time clamping is a robust safety net.

followUps.question: How would you handle pagination for a dataset too large to load at once?
followUps.answer: Switch to server-side pagination: send the current page and page size to the API and render only the returned page, along with a total count to compute totalPages. The component holds just the current page of data and the page number, issuing a new request on page change. This keeps memory and transfer bounded regardless of total dataset size.

question: Build infinite scroll that loads more items as the user reaches the bottom.
thoughtProcess: Infinite scroll loads the next batch when a sentinel element near the bottom becomes visible. The modern approach is IntersectionObserver, which is more efficient than scroll listeners. I'll keep the accumulated items, the current page, a loading flag, and a hasMore flag. I attach a ref to a sentinel div at the end of the list, observe it, and when it intersects and we're not already loading and there's more, I fetch the next page and append. I must avoid double-fetching by guarding on loading, and clean up the observer. I'll use a callback ref or set up the observer in an effect.
lineByLine: items accumulates all loaded items, page is the current page, loading guards against concurrent fetches, hasMore signals whether more pages exist, and sentinelRef points at the bottom marker. The first effect fetches whenever page changes, appends the new items immutably, sets hasMore based on whether the batch was empty, and uses a cancelled flag so a late response after unmount or page change is ignored. The second effect creates an IntersectionObserver on the sentinel; when the sentinel scrolls into view and we are neither loading nor out of data, it advances the page, which triggers the fetch effect. The observer is disconnected on cleanup. The sentinel is only rendered while hasMore is true.
timeComplexity: O(b) per load to append a batch of size b; rendering is O(n) in total items.
spaceComplexity: O(n) since all loaded items are kept in memory.

alternativeApproaches.title: Scroll event listener with throttling
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Before IntersectionObserver, you'd listen to scroll, compare scrollTop plus clientHeight to scrollHeight near the bottom, and throttle the handler. It works but is less efficient and more error-prone than the observer.

alternativeApproaches.title: Combine with virtualization
alternativeApproaches.explanation: For very long infinite lists, pair infinite scroll with a virtualization library so the DOM holds only visible rows even as thousands of items accumulate in state, keeping scroll performance high.

followUps.question: Why use IntersectionObserver instead of a scroll event listener?
followUps.answer: IntersectionObserver fires asynchronously only when the observed element's visibility crosses a threshold, off the main scroll path, so it avoids the performance cost and jank of running a handler on every scroll event. It also requires less manual math comparing scroll positions and is less error-prone. Scroll listeners can work but need throttling and careful boundary calculations.

followUps.question: How do you prevent loading the same page twice?
followUps.answer: Guard the trigger with the loading flag so a new page is only requested when a fetch isn't already in progress, and gate on hasMore so you stop at the end. Advancing page through the functional updater and driving the fetch off page changes also ensures one fetch per page. The cancelled flag additionally discards stale responses if the component unmounts mid-request.

question: Fetch data on mount and handle loading, error, and success states.
thoughtProcess: The standard pattern is three pieces of state: data, loading, and error, plus an effect that runs on mount. I set loading true, fetch, and on success store data, on failure store the error, and clear loading in both cases. I must check response.ok because fetch only rejects on network errors, not HTTP error statuses. I'll guard against setting state after unmount using a cancelled flag or AbortController, and render the three states distinctly so the UI is clear. This is the foundation for a reusable useFetch hook.
lineByLine: We hold data, loading initialized true, and error. The effect runs on mount and whenever userId changes, resetting loading and error first. It fetches, throws if response.ok is false so HTTP errors reach the catch, parses JSON, stores data on success, stores the error on failure, and clears loading in finally. Each state setter is guarded by the cancelled flag, set true in cleanup, so a response that resolves after the component unmounts or userId changes does not set state, avoiding warnings and stale updates. The render returns distinct UI for loading, error, and success.
timeComplexity: Dominated by the network request; state updates are O(1).
spaceComplexity: O(n) in the size of the fetched data.

alternativeApproaches.title: Use AbortController to cancel the request
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Instead of a cancelled flag, pass an AbortController signal to fetch and abort it in cleanup, which actually cancels the in-flight request rather than just ignoring its result.

alternativeApproaches.title: Use a data-fetching library
alternativeApproaches.explanation: TanStack Query or SWR provide caching, retries, deduplication, and built-in loading and error states, removing most of this boilerplate and handling edge cases like refetch on focus.

followUps.question: Why must you check response.ok when using fetch?
followUps.answer: fetch only rejects its promise on network-level failures like a dropped connection. An HTTP error status such as 404 or 500 still resolves successfully with ok false. If you don't check response.ok, you'd try to parse an error body as if it were valid data and silently treat failures as success. Throwing when ok is false routes HTTP errors into the catch block where they belong.

followUps.question: Why is the cancelled flag or AbortController necessary?
followUps.answer: If the component unmounts or userId changes while a request is in flight, the response may resolve afterward and call setState on a stale or unmounted component, which is wasteful and can cause out-of-order updates where an older request overwrites a newer one. The cancelled flag makes late responses no-ops, and an AbortController goes further by actually cancelling the request. Both keep the displayed data consistent with the current props.

question: Write a custom useFetch hook that returns data, loading, and error.
thoughtProcess: I'll extract the fetch-with-states pattern into a reusable hook. It takes a URL and returns data, loading, and error. Inside, I keep the three state pieces and an effect keyed on the URL that fetches, handles HTTP errors via response.ok, and guards against stale updates with an AbortController. Returning a stable shape lets any component consume it. I should reset loading and error when the URL changes, and ignore AbortError in the catch so a deliberate cancellation isn't surfaced as an error. I'll keep the options minimal but mention extensibility.
lineByLine: The hook holds data, loading defaulted true, and error. The effect, keyed on url, creates an AbortController, resets loading and error, and fetches with the abort signal. It throws on a non-ok response so HTTP errors reach catch, parses JSON, and stores data. In catch it ignores AbortError, which is the expected outcome of a deliberate cancel, and stores real errors. finally clears loading unless the request was aborted. Cleanup aborts the request when url changes or on unmount, preventing stale updates and out-of-order responses. The hook returns the three values, and the consuming Repos component branches on them.
timeComplexity: Dominated by the network request; the hook's own work is O(1).
spaceComplexity: O(n) in the fetched data size.

alternativeApproaches.title: Add a refetch function and a reducer
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Return a refetch callback and manage state with useReducer so the loading, success, and error transitions are atomic and a manual reload is possible.

alternativeApproaches.title: Adopt TanStack Query
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Rather than hand-rolling, useQuery from TanStack Query gives caching, background refetching, retries, and dedup out of the box, which a custom useFetch would need significant work to match.

followUps.question: Why catch and ignore AbortError specifically?
followUps.answer: When the cleanup calls controller.abort, the in-flight fetch rejects with an AbortError. That rejection is expected and not a real failure, so surfacing it as an error in state would incorrectly show an error message during normal navigation or URL changes. Filtering it out in the catch keeps the error state reserved for genuine failures.

followUps.question: What's a subtle bug with passing an options object to useFetch?
followUps.answer: If callers pass an inline options object, it is a new reference each render. If options were in the effect's dependency array, the effect would refire every render, causing an infinite fetch loop. The example keys the effect only on url to avoid this, but that means options changes are ignored. A robust hook would memoize or serialize options, or document that options must be stable, to handle both correctness and avoiding the loop.

question: Write a custom useDebounce hook that returns a debounced value.
thoughtProcess: The hook takes a value and a delay and returns a debounced copy that updates only after the value has stopped changing for the delay. Inside, I keep the debounced value in state and an effect that, on each value change, sets a timer to update it; the cleanup clears the previous timer, which is what produces the debounce. The dependency array includes value and delay. This is a clean, widely reused hook, and I'll show it driving a search so the usage is concrete.
lineByLine: useDebounce initializes the debounced value to the current value. Its effect runs whenever value or delay changes: it schedules setDebounced(value) after the delay, and the cleanup clears that timer before the next run. Because rapid value changes keep clearing and rescheduling the timer, debounced only updates once the value has been stable for the full delay. The hook returns debounced. In Search, the raw query updates immediately on every keystroke for a responsive input, while the effect that performs the search depends on debouncedQuery, so it only runs after typing pauses.
timeComplexity: O(1) per value change to schedule the timer.

alternativeApproaches.title: Debounce a callback instead of a value
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Sometimes you want a debounced function rather than a debounced value. A useDebouncedCallback hook stores the callback in a ref and returns a stable debounced wrapper, useful for event handlers like save-on-type.

alternativeApproaches.title: Leading-edge debounce
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Add an option to fire immediately on the first call and then debounce subsequent ones, which suits actions where the first event should feel instant.

followUps.question: Why does clearing the timer in the cleanup create the debounce effect?
followUps.answer: Each time value changes, React runs the effect cleanup before the new effect. The cleanup clears the timer scheduled by the previous run, cancelling its pending update. So as long as value keeps changing within the delay, every scheduled update is cancelled before it fires, and only when value stays unchanged for the full delay does a timer survive to update the debounced value. That cancel-and-reschedule cycle is exactly debouncing.

followUps.question: What is the difference between debouncing a value and a callback?
followUps.answer: Debouncing a value, as in useDebounce, gives you a state value that lags behind the source; you typically react to it in an effect. Debouncing a callback gives you a function that, when called repeatedly, only actually executes after calls stop, which suits direct event handling like firing a save. The value version integrates naturally with React's render-and-effect flow; the callback version is handier when you want to wrap an imperative action.

question: Write a custom useLocalStorage hook that syncs state with localStorage.
thoughtProcess: The hook should behave like useState but persist to localStorage under a key. I'll initialize state lazily by reading and parsing from localStorage once, falling back to a provided initial value, and wrapping in try/catch since storage access and JSON parsing can throw. I'll return a setter that updates both React state and localStorage, supporting the functional updater form like useState. I'll write to storage in an effect or inside the setter; doing it in the setter keeps React state authoritative. I should guard against storage being unavailable, for example in private mode.
lineByLine: useState is given a lazy initializer that runs only on mount: it reads the key from localStorage, parses it if present, and otherwise uses initialValue, all inside try/catch so a parse error or unavailable storage falls back to the initial value. setValue mirrors useState's API: it accepts either a value or an updater function, computes the next value using the previous state, writes the serialized value to localStorage inside try/catch so a quota or private-mode error doesn't crash the app, and returns next so React state updates. The hook returns the tuple, so Settings consumes it exactly like useState while persisting across reloads.
timeComplexity: O(s) per read and write where s is the serialized size, due to JSON parse and stringify.
spaceComplexity: O(s) for the stored value in memory and storage.

alternativeApproaches.title: Sync across tabs with the storage event
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Listen to the window storage event so changes made in another tab update this tab's state, keeping multiple tabs consistent.

alternativeApproaches.title: Write in an effect instead of the setter
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Persist with a useEffect keyed on the value, which decouples the write from the setter and naturally writes after every state change, though it adds a render before the write.

followUps.question: Why initialize with the lazy function form of useState here?
followUps.answer: Reading and parsing from localStorage is comparatively expensive and only needs to happen once. The lazy initializer, a function passed to useState, runs only on the first render, so the read and JSON.parse don't repeat on every render. Passing the parsed value directly would re-read storage on every render, wasting work.

followUps.question: Why wrap the storage access in try/catch?
followUps.answer: localStorage can throw: it may be disabled or in a restricted mode where access throws, writes can exceed the quota, and a stored value might be malformed JSON that JSON.parse rejects. Wrapping in try/catch lets the app degrade gracefully, falling back to the initial value on read failure and keeping state in memory on write failure, rather than crashing the component.

question: Build a stopwatch with start, stop, and reset.
thoughtProcess: A stopwatch tracks elapsed time and whether it's running. The naive approach uses setInterval to increment a counter, but interval drift makes it inaccurate over time. A more accurate approach records the start timestamp and computes elapsed as now minus start, ticking the interval only to trigger re-renders. I'll keep it approachable with the accumulated-time pattern: store elapsed plus a running flag, and on each tick add the delta. I'll store the interval id in a ref so it survives renders and can be cleared. Start sets running, stop clears the interval, reset zeros everything. Cleanup clears the interval on unmount.
lineByLine: elapsed is milliseconds elapsed, running is whether the clock is ticking, and intervalRef holds the interval id across renders without causing re-renders. The effect runs when running changes: if running, it computes a start timestamp as now minus the already-elapsed time so resuming continues from where it stopped, then sets an interval that updates elapsed to the real time difference, which avoids interval drift. The cleanup clears the interval whenever running flips or on unmount. Start and Stop toggle running and are disabled appropriately. Reset stops and zeroes elapsed. Display divides by 1000 for seconds.
timeComplexity: O(1) per tick; ticks fire at the interval rate.

alternativeApproaches.title: Naive interval counter
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Increment elapsed by a fixed amount each tick with setInterval. Simpler to read but accumulates drift, since intervals are not guaranteed to fire exactly on schedule, so it loses accuracy over minutes.

alternativeApproaches.title: requestAnimationFrame loop
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Use requestAnimationFrame instead of setInterval for display updates synced to the screen refresh, computing elapsed from timestamps, which is smooth and pauses when the tab is hidden.

followUps.question: Why store the interval id in a ref instead of state?
followUps.answer: The interval id is a mutable value we need to persist across renders to clear it later, but changing it should not trigger a re-render. A ref is exactly that: a stable container whose .current can be updated without causing renders. Putting it in state would cause unnecessary re-renders and the asynchronous nature of state updates would make it awkward to read the current id in cleanup.

followUps.question: Why is computing elapsed from timestamps more accurate than incrementing a counter?
followUps.answer: setInterval does not fire exactly on schedule; under load or in a background tab, ticks are delayed and skipped, so incrementing a counter by a fixed amount each tick drifts away from real time. Computing elapsed as the difference between the current timestamp and the recorded start time always reflects true wall-clock elapsed time regardless of when ticks actually fire, so the interval only drives re-renders, not the time calculation.

question: Build a light/dark theme toggle using Context.
thoughtProcess: I'll create a ThemeContext and a provider that holds the current theme and a toggle function, persisting the choice to localStorage and applying it to the document so CSS can react. Consumers read the theme via a custom useTheme hook that throws if used outside the provider, a good guardrail. I'll memoize the context value so consumers don't re-render when the provider re-renders for unrelated reasons. An effect applies the theme to a data attribute on the root element. This separates state from presentation and is a clean, reusable pattern.
lineByLine: ThemeContext is created with a null default so the hook can detect misuse. ThemeProvider initializes theme lazily from localStorage, defaulting to light. An effect applies the theme to a data-theme attribute on the root html element, which CSS can target, and persists it to localStorage whenever theme changes. The provider value is memoized with useMemo keyed on theme, so its reference is stable unless theme actually changes, preventing consumers from re-rendering when the provider re-renders for unrelated reasons. useTheme reads the context and throws a clear error if used outside the provider. ThemeToggle consumes the hook and flips the theme on click.

alternativeApproaches.title: Respect the system preference
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Default to the user's OS setting via the prefers-color-scheme media query when no stored choice exists, and listen for changes so the app follows the system theme until the user overrides it.
alternativeApproaches.code:
const prefersDark = window.matchMedia('(prefers-color-scheme: dark)').matches;
const initial = localStorage.getItem('theme') || (prefersDark ? 'dark' : 'light');

alternativeApproaches.title: Split state and toggle into two contexts
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Provide the theme value and the toggle function in separate contexts so components that only call toggle never re-render when the theme value changes, a fine-grained optimization for large trees.

followUps.question: Why memoize the context value with useMemo?
followUps.answer: The provider's value is an object literal, which would be a new reference on every provider render. Since every context consumer re-renders when the value reference changes, an unmemoized inline object would re-render all consumers whenever the provider re-renders, even for unrelated reasons. Wrapping the value in useMemo keyed on theme keeps the reference stable unless theme actually changes, so consumers only re-render on real theme changes.

followUps.question: Why does useTheme throw when used outside the provider?
followUps.answer: The context default is null, so calling useTheme outside a ThemeProvider returns null and any attempt to read theme or toggleTheme would crash with an unclear error elsewhere. Throwing an explicit error immediately gives a precise, actionable message about the missing provider, turning a confusing runtime failure into a clear developer-facing one. This is a common defensive pattern for context-backed hooks.

question: Build a data table with sortable columns.
thoughtProcess: I need rows of data, a set of columns, and sort state: which column key and the direction. Clicking a header sets the sort key, or flips direction if it's already the active key. The sorted rows are derived from the data and sort config, so I compute them during render, ideally memoized since sorting can be costly. I'll write a comparator that handles ascending and descending, and avoid mutating the original array by copying before sort. I'll show a sort indicator in the active header. For large datasets I'd combine with virtualization, which I'll note.
lineByLine: sort holds the active column key and direction. sortedRows is memoized with useMemo keyed on rows and sort, so the potentially expensive sort only runs when the data or sort config changes, not on unrelated re-renders. It returns the rows unsorted when no key is set, otherwise copies the array with spread before sorting to avoid mutating the prop, and compares using the active key and direction. handleSort toggles direction if the same column header is clicked again, or starts a fresh ascending sort on a new column. The header cells trigger sorting and show an indicator on the active column; the body renders the sorted rows keyed by a stable id, with cells driven by the column definitions.
timeComplexity: O(n log n) per sort over n rows, memoized so it only reruns when rows or sort change.
spaceComplexity: O(n) for the copied, sorted array.

alternativeApproaches.title: Custom comparators per column
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Let each column define a sortFn so numbers, dates, and strings sort correctly, since the default less-than comparison mishandles mixed or locale-sensitive data.

alternativeApproaches.title: Server-side sorting with virtualization
alternativeApproaches.explanation: For very large tables, sort on the server via query params and render only visible rows with a virtualization library, so neither sorting nor rendering blocks the main thread on the full dataset.

followUps.question: Why copy the array before calling sort?
followUps.answer: Array.prototype.sort mutates the array in place. The rows array comes from props, and mutating props or state directly violates React's immutability expectations: it can cause stale reference comparisons, defeat memoization, and produce confusing bugs where the source data changes unexpectedly. Spreading into a new array first means we sort a copy and leave the original rows untouched, returning a fresh array React can detect.

followUps.question: Why wrap the sort in useMemo, and what are its dependencies?
followUps.answer: Sorting is O(n log n) and can be expensive for large tables, and the component may re-render for reasons unrelated to the data or sort config. useMemo keyed on rows and sort ensures the sort only recomputes when the underlying data or the sort key/direction actually change, skipping the work on unrelated re-renders. The dependency array must include rows and sort because those are the inputs the computation reads; omitting either would yield a stale sorted result.
